breaking: Space: October's full moon, the Hunter's Moon, will be full on Sunday night in Peru.

articles.headline: Look up! The Hunter's Moon is coming
articles.standfirst: October's full moon has a special name. You can see it this weekend.
body: Every month there is a full moon, and many full moons have old names. The full moon in October is called the Hunter's Moon. A long time ago, after people finished collecting food from their fields in autumn, hunters used the bright light of the moon to find animals at night.
This year, the moon will be full at 11.11 p.m. on Sunday 25 October in Peru. But you don't need to wait for that minute. The moon will also look full the night before and the night after.
The best time to look is in the evening, when the moon comes up. At that time it is low in the sky, in the east.

There are 13 full moons in 2026, not 12, and the Hunter's Moon is number 11. The next two full moons, on 24 November and 23 December, are supermoons. They are the closest and brightest full moons of the year.

articles.headline: A new plant with almost black flowers
articles.standfirst: Scientists have found a new plant in and near Manu National Park. Its name comes from the Andean bear.
body: Scientists from the Peruvian group Conservación Amazónica have found a new kind of plant in Manu National Park and the area around it, in Cusco. The plant is a bromeliad, and its name is Puya ukumari.
The plant can grow up to two metres tall. Its petals are a very dark blue, so they look almost black. It lives in the mountains, between 2,300 and 3,300 metres high.
Why ukumari? This word means 'bear' in Quechua. The scientists studied the food of Andean bears, and this helped them to find more of the plants.

Scientists first saw the plant in 2022, and they found the first plant with flowers in August 2025. They think it is in danger because fires, farm animals and landslides are damaging the places where it grows.

articles.headline: A baby giant: what a tiny whale shark could teach scientists
articles.standfirst: Fishers in Indonesia found a whale shark only 1.5 metres long. It could help to solve a big mystery about the world's largest fish.
body: On 6 September 2024, fishers in Saleh Bay, on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa, found something unusual in their net: a whale shark. Whale sharks are the largest fish in the world and can grow to more than 12 metres, but this one was only about 1.5 metres long. Scientists worked out that it was about four months old.

It was the first newborn whale shark ever recorded in Indonesia, and only about 33 have been found anywhere in the world. That is why the discovery is so exciting. Scientists know a lot about adult whale sharks, which can travel thousands of kilometres, but nobody has ever seen one being born in the wild.

Saleh Bay could be a kind of nursery. It is almost closed off from the open ocean, mangroves grow around much of it, and it has plenty of plankton and krill for the sharks to eat. A young shark is also safer there, because some predators can attack a small shark but not a huge adult. However, researchers still don't know if the baby was born in the bay or swam there later.

Local people's feelings about whale sharks are changing too. Fishers once saw them as rivals that took their fish, but today young people take tourists out on boats to see them. A conservation group, Konservasi Indonesia, is working to create a protected area for whale sharks in the north of the bay.

articles.headline: Two clay figures from Caral, one of the oldest cities in the Americas
articles.standfirst: Archaeologists have found two small figures that are between 3,800 and 5,000 years old. They may show how the people of Caral saw the world.
body: Archaeologists working at Caral, an ancient city about four hours north of Lima, have found two small figures made of clay. They were discovered in a building near the Main Residential Complex of the Sacred City of Caral, and experts think they were made between 3000 and 1800 BC.

One figure is a man and the other is a woman, so they may represent a couple. Marco Antonio Machacuay, an archaeologist at the Caral Archaeological Zone, told the news agency Andina that the figures could show how the people of Caral thought about nature and about themselves. Figures like these are not found in many places, which makes them especially interesting.

The early figures had no colour. People in Caral made white figures of men, women, animals and plants, with many details of everyday life. After 1800 BC, they started to add colours, especially to clothes and jewellery, and female figures became more common and more symbolic.

Because they are so old and delicate, the two figures were shown for only a short time in an exhibition about Caral at the Ministry of Culture in Lima. This month Caral also celebrates 32 years since research began there. On 23 and 24 October there will be a ceremony for Pachamama, coloured lights on the old buildings at night, and a cultural festival with traditional dancers.

articles.headline: Not less creative, just less confident: what children and adults reveal about imagination
articles.standfirst: A new study suggests that adults produce more original work than young children – but feel far more anxious while they do it.
body: Give a five-year-old a paintbrush and they will usually start painting straight away; give one to an adult and there is often a pause. It is widely assumed that this is because children are simply more creative. A new study, published in the journal Plos One, suggests that the real explanation is rather different.

Researchers from the University of Graz in Austria, working with UCLouvain in Belgium and Yale University in the United States, compared 92 children aged four to seven with 70 adults, most of them in their twenties. Everyone completed three tasks: thinking of as many creative uses for a tin as possible in three minutes, drawing anything they liked with no time limit, and drawing an imaginary animal in eight minutes.

Judges then rated the results for originality, usefulness and overall creativity. The adults' work scored higher, especially when the task had a clear goal and a time limit. Yet when participants described their feelings, the pattern was reversed: the children said they felt more confident and motivated, and less anxious, than the adults did.

According to Dr Mathias Benedek, the study's senior author, we often mistake children's total absorption in play for greater creative ability. Children enjoy the process and treat mistakes as part of it, he explained, while adults focus more on the result and, worried about being judged, often reject unusual ideas before they have even tried them.

The study has its limits. It compared only two age groups at a single moment, so it cannot show how creativity changes as people grow older, and young children tend to choose extreme answers on rating scales. Even so, the researchers believe the popular idea that creativity fades with age is mistaken. As Benedek put it, adults "don't lose their creativity" – they lose the confidence to use it.

articles.instructions: For each question, choose the paragraph (A–E). Each paragraph can be chosen once.
articles.headline: A host's headache: how the Asian Games in Japan went wrong
articles.standfirst: Japan has a reputation for running major events smoothly, but this year's Asian Games in Nagoya will be remembered for a long list of mistakes.
body: A. Japan has hosted the Olympics and attracts huge crowds to events such as Tokyo's annual video game show, so expectations were high for this year's Asian Games in Nagoya and the surrounding Aichi Prefecture. Instead, the event was hit by one problem after another, and some people online even called it the worst Games in history.

B. Trouble began before any competition had started. To keep costs down, the organisers had decided not to build a traditional athletes' village and put participants in hotels and container-style units instead. A senior Korean basketball official complained that tall players in the containers could not stretch out their legs in bed. When more sports were added, the number of people needing rooms rose by 2,000 to about 17,000, and an Italian cruise ship with 1,500 cabins was brought in to fill the gap.

C. During the Games, the mistakes kept coming. Some athletes were taken by bus to the wrong venues, the North Korean anthem was played for South Korea's men's hockey team, and the South Korean flag was not raised properly at the men's football medal ceremony. Officials later had to send South Korea a formal apology.

D. Much of the criticism has focused on the company that ran the venues, the Japanese branch of the French firm GL Events, which won a contract worth 63 billion yen. A Japanese newspaper claimed the firm had cut corners by hiring too few experienced staff. However, the deputy director general of the Games, Takaaki Omi, pointed out that the company had worked on the Paris Olympics.

E. Kozo Tomiyama, a professor at Osaka University who studies sporting events, believes the organisers simply could not cope with the unexpected. He warned that if other countries lose confidence in Japan's ability to run such events, it may become harder for Japan to attract international competitions in the future.

articles.headline: Hidden in plain sight: how AI exposed a weakness at the heart of the web
articles.standfirst: Two flaws in PHP, the programming language behind a huge share of the world's websites, went unnoticed for over a decade – until artificial intelligence found them.
body: Few people outside the technology industry have heard of PHP, yet most of us rely on it every day. Created in the early 1990s, it is an open-source language that runs on web servers and assembles the pages we see in our browsers. Wikipedia, countless online shops and WordPress, the system behind a vast number of websites, all depend on it; the cyber-security firm Wiz estimates that it powers 70% of the world's websites.

This week, researchers from Wiz and another firm, Calif, revealed two serious vulnerabilities, nicknamed "php2shell", built into the language itself and present in versions released over the past decade. Under the right conditions, attackers could exploit them to take control of a web server and steal sensitive data. Strikingly, the flaws were uncovered with the help of technology from OpenAI, which described the discovery as one of the most significant security problems in recent memory.

The response was swift. The PHP Foundation, the non-profit organisation that maintains the language, released patches on Wednesday and urged all users to update immediately. Security agencies in the United States, the UK, the EU, Singapore and Australia issued warnings, and the US National Security Agency told organisations that could not patch their systems straight away to take them offline. In Japan, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi asked people to check whether their public websites ran on PHP. Wikimedia, the Finnish government and several Scottish councils were among those that temporarily took sites or services down.

Experts fear the danger is far from over. Now that technical details are being made public, further attempts to exploit the flaws are likely, and poorly maintained websites run by small organisations with limited security resources are especially exposed. One security executive also warned that AI could make such attacks faster and easier to carry out.

Therein lies an uncomfortable irony. The kind of technology that brought these long-buried weaknesses to light could equally help criminals to find and exploit similar ones. Whether AI ultimately makes the internet safer may depend less on the tools themselves than on who uses them first – and how quickly defenders respond.

articles.headline: Paying nature back? A billion-dollar fund that has collected almost nothing
articles.standfirst: A global fund designed to share the profits made from nature's genetic information has received only a few thousand dollars, and drug companies are under pressure.
body: Many modern medicines owe something to nature. Researchers increasingly work with genetic information taken from organisms around the world, much of it now stored as digital sequence information (DSI) in public databases. The Cali Fund was set up so that some of the profits made from that information would flow back into conservation, particularly in low-income countries, with at least half of the money going to priorities chosen by Indigenous peoples and local communities. The target was ambitious: $1 billion a year.

More than 18 months after its official launch in February 2025, the reality looks very different. By Monday, when the Cop17 biodiversity summit opened in Yerevan, the capital of Armenia, the fund had received just $10,656 in commitments, of which $7,085 had actually been paid. All of it came from three small firms in the UK and Belgium; not one major pharmaceutical company had contributed.

The fund asks companies to give, voluntarily, 1% of their profits or 0.1% of their revenue. According to an analysis by Zero Carbon Analytics, had the 15 largest drug companies followed that guideline, they could have contributed $756 million based on last year's results – a modest sum next to the roughly $161 billion in profits they made in 2025. Critics accuse the industry of "free-riding" on nature, and one campaigner observed that more money had been spent on meetings about the fund than the fund itself contained.

The industry rejects that portrayal. Its international federation insists it is committed to biodiversity but argues that the fund overlaps with existing laws and demands a share of total revenue whether or not DSI was used to develop a given medicine. A spokesperson for the fund, meanwhile, called the result disappointing but not entirely surprising, noting that similar schemes have typically taken two to three years before contributions grew.

The underlying question is whether voluntary schemes can ever deliver. Some campaigners argue that companies should be compelled to pay; others hope that discussions at Cop17 will persuade businesses to come forward. With a $700 billion gap in global funding for nature conservation, a great deal rides on the answer.
